name: Light Periwinkle
lede: Light Periwinkle is a pale greyish blue-violet that four separate systems have recorded since 1912, and one of our museum archive's more common named colors.

sections.title: A light build of periwinkle
sections.body:
The nearest named colors on file are [[lavender-grey]], [[pallid-blue-violet]], [[pale-neropalin-blue]] and [[pale-greyish-blue]], at 4.5, 4.7, 4.8 and 5.6 ΔE [1]. It is the oldest-recorded : Ridgway's 1912 color plates give it on plate XXIV, at hue 55 degrees, tone f, though that plate is a scan of an aged original and only approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 lists it as block 198, Wikipedia and the xkcd survey of 2010 also carry the name, and xkcd's own version of the hex runs slightly bluer, #C1C6FC [1]. 

Five ISCC-NBS near-duplicates cluster close to this swatch: Pale Campanula Blue, Periwinkle (Crayola), Fidelity, Fountain Blue and Pale Periwinkle Blue, the closest only 0.7 units away [2]. See [[periwinkle]] for the plant and the deeper blue it is usually named for.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Within CIEDE2000 4, Light Periwinkle appears in 122 of our 23,781 archive paintings (0.51%), making it more common than 56% of our named colors, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 14 of 1,674 paintings from that century, about 1.8 times the archive's overall rate [3]. Within a painting it most often sits in the lights, in 53% of the 83 paintings where our within-painting lens finds it [3]. John Singer Sargent carries it in 4 of his 287 archive paintings, the most of any single painter, though not enough to stand out against the museum baseline [3]. The earliest match is a 1414 panel by Lorenzo Monaco, nearly five centuries before the name's earliest record in our sources (1912); that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that anyone called it Light Periwinkle at the time, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. In print, the word rose fastest in the 2000s, across all its senses, including the plant and the place as well as the color [3].
